segments.text: 9-11. I mean, we did of course see the destruction of Al Qaeda, we saw the killing of Osama bin
Laden, we saw the US pull out of Afghanistan, but in your mind is what we are seeing now
in the Middle East some way of a continuation of that war on terror or is it something
else? Is it something new?
Well, I think it is partly a continuation of it. Yeah. We saw, as you say, the defeat of Al
Qaeda, but then of course we had Al Qaeda in Iraq, which kind of grew out of it. There was
a claim of victory against Al Qaeda in Iraq. But then we had ISIS, which which grew
to a large extent out of Al Qaeda in Iraq. So you have this sort of serial declaration
of victories. And then people can relax for a little bit. But then something else happens.
And a lot of times these threats are feeding into each other. There's a continuity
between these organizations. I think, you know, the destruction of Gaza, you know,
that is in a way a very distinct problem. But it was an action that was presented by
Israel within the framework of a war on terror. In Sri Lanka, where I was in 2009,
you know, the government wreaked horrible destruction on the Tamil population in the
name of an international war on terror. And it was actually difficult for Britain or
the United States to criticize that. You know, when they themselves were detaining
people indefinitely, they themselves had the language of the war on terror. And we need
to be ruthless. We need to suspend liberty to a certain extent in the interest of
security.
Specifically on the language used around the war on terror, I guess a very seismic
symbolic shift at least came with the rebranding of the Secretary of Defense to
the Secretary of War, the Defense Department to the War Department. Because I mean,
that signaled almost a kind of move away from more of a reactive war on terror to a US
administration that sought to project power to pursue a peace through strength, I think
is the words used by by Pete Hegseth. So do you see that as a rebranding of what's
gone before? Or is that really a defining departure from what we've seen in the
past?
I think it's a great question. I think it is partly rebranding. But it's partly
an indication that violence and the assertion of America's right in particular
to do what it's like to do what it likes has become sort of incredibly
shameless under Trump. And Trump is somebody really who has systematically
rejected shame and indeed made a lot of political capital, in my opinion, out
of offering people a kind of vicarious shamelessness through his abuses and
through his spectacular demonstrations of freedom, as I say, freedom for for
himself. So I think, you know, there are some significant differences. For
example, George W. Bush and Tony Blair, you know, they did make some efforts to
try to create some sense of international legitimacy for what they
wanted to do in Iraq, and to try and get the UN on board to a certain extent.
We're not seeing that now with Trump and Netanyahu. We're just seeing a kind of
go it alone spirit, which I think is incredibly dangerous and incredibly
destructive. So I do think there's a shamelessness about what's going on.
And that thing you mentioned about relabeling as a department of war,
you know, Trump would say, well, this is, you know, this is honesty. You know,
he projects this image of honesty. I'm not a hypocrite. The liberals are
hypocrites. I tell you the truth as it is. And he's made some considerable
political capital out of that, in my opinion. But it's also a very frightening
turn.
David, talking about political capital, we've talked about the big powers.
I'd like to talk about the small powers, if I may, because I wonder if the
rise of non-state actors, Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Houthis in Yemen,
whether they fit into this into this frame as well, because I want to know if
they are motivated by the same impulses that perhaps Iran or the United
States may be for their own ends. I mean, how does your approach to
this work when war is being waged by smaller paramilitary networks? Okay,
some see Hezbollah as being almost a kind of mini-franchise of Iran in the same
way that you would view the branch of a bank internationally. But is that a
wrong way of looking at this?
Well, I think a lot of these non-state actors, you know, they do very often
have state backers, you know, and we've seen it with Hezbollah. We've
seen it with the rapid support forces and the UAE in Sudan. So we can't sort
of regard them simply as non-state actors. I think that, you know, in the case
of Hezbollah in Lebanon, you know, there has been quite a strong effort
from the Lebanese government to weaken Hezbollah. And that's something
that can potentially, I think, bear a lot of fruit. And then when Israel comes
in and starts bombing Lebanon and displacing, you know, as I understand
it, a million people, you know, this can easily set things back. So the
states tend to sort of weigh in on these struggles, these local
struggles, often in extremely counterproductive ways. I think Sudan, you
know, is an interesting case of a government that, you know, going back
to the 1980s, tried to mobilize militias, mobilize his own militias for the
purposes of counterinsurgency. But then the government, in a way, lost
control of the violence because the militias were economically motivated to
a large extent. They spread rebellion to new areas. And on the whole, they
refused to disband after particular military campaigns. And they became, as
were, a political factor in their own right. And we know that the RSF, you
know, is a successor to the Janjaweed militias that created the Darfur
genocide. And it's been a huge factor in Sudan politics ever since, you
know, basically extorting the government, using gold in particular to
build up its strength, and eventually turning against the army with the
result of this horrific civil war that we have at the moment. So
militias don't always obey what their puppet masters tell them to do. And
that can be very destructive in itself.
David, can a conflict like the Iran-Israel rivalry ever truly end, taking
in everything you've discussed? Or does that system, does that system
simply evolve into new forms of hybrid warfare, or to protect
essentially underlying profit margins and existing power structures?
Well, I think conflicts can come to an end. I think a lot of people
thought that the Cold War would never end, because partly of the vested
interests enfold. But it did actually surprise us by ending. Of
course, people who were making the argument that it will never end
will now point to various aspects of a revival of the Cold War, you
know, in terms of Russia, and even China, and so on. So I do
think sometimes that violence is a little bit like energy, you know, in
the sense that it can change from one form to another. But it very
rarely disappears entirely. In practice, I think, you know, one of
the things you can do is to make peace more profitable and more
attractive for various warring parties than war itself, you
know, can offer them a stake in a political settlement in a
peace process, you can buy them off if you like. One of the
problems with that, of course, is that you are you tend to
entrench corruption and indeed violence within the peace
settlement that you're actually creating or offering.
David, in a fragmented global economy, I mean, how does the
political conflict of those big powers, the political conflict
that we are seeing play out in the Middle East? I mean, how does
that affect the global south? How does that affect nations that
are watching from the sidelines or simultaneously protecting the

know that oil prices are going up. We know that fertilizer
prices have been drastically affected. This affects food
production and it affects people's food security. And I think,
you know, if we go back in history just a little bit to, for
example, 2011, you know, you had a huge increase in global food
prices for various reasons. And that fed rather directly into
famine in places like Yemen and Somalia. And it also fed
into the so-called Arab Spring and the Civil War in Syria,
for example. So these kind of knock-on effects, you know,
that they're not always predictable, but I think you can predict
that many of them are going to be extremely bad and the people
that are going to suffer are going to be, you know, very far
from from Washington or Jerusalem. David King, thank you
for talking to Al Jazeera.
Yeah, pleasure to talk to you.
